awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: Biodegradable Microencapsulation for Agrochemicals
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader/commercial impact of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project is to develop biodegradable microencapsulation technology for agrochemicals. Microencapsulation technology is used for dispersion and controlled-delivery in certain agrochemicals. However, traditional microencapsulation materials in these products made from non-biodegradable polymers can cause microplastic pollution, which has become a critical environmental concern.  The agrochemical sector has an urgent need for new microencapsulation technology with biodegradable materials. This project explores using plant-based materials to replace the plastic-based materials in traditional process, and expands the capability to encapsulate a broader range of agrochemicals with different properties. Compared to other emerging solutions, the proposed technology provides competitive cost and environmentally-friendly procedure. In addition to meeting the regulatory requirement, it can benefit a large potential market by reducing the degradation and runoff of agrochemicals in the field to ensure high efficiency. By using microencapsulation to extend the retention time and enable the slow-release process, the proposed technology can make more effective use of agrochemicals while substantially mitigating their impact.

This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project involves creating microencapsulation methods with plant-based biodegradable materials to encapsulate both hydrophobic and hydrophilic agrochemical ingredients. Conventional technologies for encapsulating oil-based ingredients use interfacial polymerization mechanism. Given that a limited number of chemical reactions can form a polymer layer at water/oil interface, the resulting shell materials are prevalently non-biodegradable polymers. The proposed technology is based on a new mechanism with an amphiphilic polymer crosslinked in situ to form the shell. The materials are derived from natural materials such as polysaccharides and fatty acids that have intrinsic biodegradability. To encapsulate hydrophilic compounds, this project will explore bilayer shell structure and coacervation methods. The encapsulation will be based on the factors of electrical charge, polarity or steric effect of the molecules. In order to control the release profile, the thickness of the shell will be adjusted by tuning the materials ratio and polymer structure. The stability of the microcapsule materials will be studied to ensure adequate shelf life. This project provides new scientific insights to develop microencapsulation technology with natural materials, with direct impact to address critical challenges for current agrochemical industry.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
In our NSF Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project, our research focuses on developing biodegradable microencapsulation technologies for agrochemicals. At Ultinat, Inc., our mission is to develop innovative microencapsulation platforms that reduce microplastic pollution, protect active ingredients, improve delivery efficiency, and enhance environmental sustainability. As regulatory restrictions on plastic-based encapsulation technologies become increasingly stringent and demand grows for biological and other novel active ingredients, our technology addresses these evolving market needs by providing new solutions to the critical technical challenges. In previous research, we developed a proprietary microencapsulation method with biodegradable materials for oil-based ingredients, providing an effective solution to the urgent issues of microplastic pollution. Building on this foundation, the Phase I project extends the technology to encapsulate hydrophilic active ingredients, including biological ingredients, with the goals of enhancing their stability, protecting them from environmental degradation, and improving their delivery efficiency. The new encapsulation strategies are designed based on the properties of the payload molecules including their solubility, molecular polarity, and electrical charges. These new approaches have achieved high and consistent encapsulation efficiency while maintaining cost-effectiveness and minimizing environmental impact.

In addition to developing new microencapsulation methods, we also conducted research on the properties of the microcapsules to evaluate their suitability for real-world applications. We studied the release profile of two traditional agrochemicals that are encapsulated with our oil-based technology. The total release amount follows a slowly increasing curve while the release speed decreases over time. The release time can vary from one week to one month depending on the agrochemicals’ dispersion status and the structure of the microcapsules. Compared to other existing technologies, our controlled release process is able to extend the release time 67% longer.

For biodegradable materials, one important performance requirement is to demonstrate sufficient stability and shelf life for end users. Although our materials have intrinsic biodegradability that allow them to degrade eventually in the soil environment, before they are applied in the field, they can be stabilized by the payload ingredients that have antimicrobial properties. Accelerated shelf-life test of a microencapsulated pesticide at 40°C for six months has proved that the ambient shelf life can achieve two years, which meets the standard shelf-life requirement for agrochemical industry. We also investigated the ability of our microencapsulation technology to protect active ingredients from ultraviolet (UV) degradation. Experimental results demonstrated that the microcapsules effectively reduce photodegradation and preserve their stability.

In order to prove the feasibility of scale-up manufacturing and adaption of the technology in the large volume manufacturing process, we increase the scale of synthesizing our proprietary polymer from grams to kilograms in one batch. By optimizing the concentrations of the reactants and improving the efficiency of the reaction, we have used standard lab equipment to complete the scaling up process and significantly reduced the reaction time.

The Phase I project successfully developed novel microencapsulation methods and addressed several key challenges associated with the commercialization of our technology. These advances have established a strong technical foundation for scaling the technology and transitioning it toward commercial production. Its successful commercialization has the potential to reduce agrochemical use, improve resource efficiency, lower production costs, and minimize environmental impacts. In addition to improving the delivery efficiency, stability, and performance of agrochemicals, the technology has broad applicability across multiple industries. Over the long term, these innovations are expected to generate substantial economic and societal benefits by supporting sustainable agriculture, enhancing crop productivity, reducing environmental pollution, and enabling the development of safer and more effective delivery systems for a wide range of new active ingredients.
